Beginner CRUD with Minimal APIs

Learn one HTTP action at a time before adding more files or a database.

Open interactive lesson and complete code

What you are building

A small student register API

Add a student, show students, change their details and remove a student. Requests send data to the API; this example has no form or webpage.

Student data is kept in memory and is lost when the app restarts.

Check the result

Send a POST request, read the new student with GET, then try PUT and DELETE.

CRUD means Create, Read, Update and Delete. Start with a small in-memory list so the HTTP ideas are easy to see before adding a database.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Install and create the right project

  • Install Visual Studio with ASP.NET and web development and a .NET 10-compatible SDK. For WPF also install .NET desktop development. Check Tools → Get Tools and Features if templates are missing.
  • Create ASP.NET Core Empty for the Minimal API, or ASP.NET Core Web API with Use controllers for a controller project. Select .NET 10. Alternatively open the supplied .csproj to get exactly the lesson files.
  • Use a separate folder for every example. Delete the generated weather sample if it conflicts with the supplied files. Restore NuGet packages before building.
  • In View → Terminal, cd into the folder containing StudyLab.csproj. For local API testing run dotnet run --urls http://localhost:5100. Open requests.http and use Send Request above each request. Use the actual port from the console if you launch with a different profile.

Your first request

GET http://localhost:5100/api/students

Initially expect 200 OK with []. A browser address bar can send GET, but cannot conveniently send all CRUD methods. Use the .http editor, Postman, curl.exe or a Swagger UI. The JSON object is a data packet, not an HTML page.

Map each operation to HTTP

POST   /api/students       # Create
GET    /api/students       # Read all
GET    /api/students/1     # Read one
PUT    /api/students/1     # Replace editable data
DELETE /api/students/1     # Delete

Expected sequence on a fresh server: GET → 200 []; POST Lefa,22 → 201 with id 1; GET /1 → 200; PUT /1 → 204 with no body; DELETE /1 → 204; GET /1 → 404. IDs can have gaps. In-memory data disappears when the app restarts.

Understand every moving part

MapGet and MapPost register routes. StudentInput is the input DTO; Student is the response record. Results.Created sets 201 and a Location header. Results.NoContent sets 204. StudentStore is registered once for this running app. ConcurrentDictionary and Interlocked make the teaching store safer for simultaneous requests. It is not a distributed database. We validate both POST and PUT, including whitespace-only names.

Try it yourself

Send an age of 2. What should happen?

Worked answer

400 Bad Request. The server must reject invalid input even if a client form also validates it.

Restart and GET all students.

Worked answer

Expect []. In-memory data is lost. The EF examples introduce persistent storage.

Predict and practise

What should GET return before any students are created?

Check your prediction

200 OK with an empty JSON array: [].

Make one change

Start with GET. Then POST a valid student and GET the returned ID. Only after that try PUT, DELETE and a final GET.

Worked guidance

Use requests.http. Expect 201 for POST, 204 for successful PUT/DELETE, and 404 when reading the deleted ID.

Try independently

Create two different students. Update one, delete the other and record each status and response.
